chapter.name: Life Processes in Animals
chapter.blurb: Digestion in humans, ruminants and birds, and breathing and respiration in humans and other animals.

concepts.name: Nutrition, the alimentary canal and digestion in the mouth
concepts.description: Life processes, the alimentary canal, mechanical digestion, saliva and its action on starch, and the food pipe.
concepts.idea: Digestion breaks complex food into simpler forms, beginning in the mouth where saliva acts on starch.
concepts.rule: Nutrition, respiration, excretion and reproduction are life processes. Animals get energy from food containing complex components such as carbohydrate, protein and fat, which must be broken down into simpler forms. This happens in the alimentary canal, a long tube from the mouth to the anus, where digestive juices secreted at different parts act on the food. In the mouth teeth crush and chew the food, called mechanical digestion. Saliva moistens food and contains a digestive juice that breaks starch into sugar, which is why chewed chapati tastes sweet. Iodine gives a blue-black colour with starch: in Activity 9.1 boiled rice turns blue-black in test tube A, while chewed rice in tube B shows little or no colour as starch has been broken down. The breaking of complex food into simpler forms is digestion. The tongue mixes food with saliva and pushes it into the food pipe (oesophagus), whose walls contract and relax in waves to push food to the stomach. Good oral hygiene prevents tooth decay.
concepts.example: Chapati tastes sweet if chewed for a long time.

concepts.name: Digestion in the stomach and small intestine
concepts.description: Stomach juices, acid and mucus, bile, pancreatic juice, and absorption in the small intestine.
concepts.idea: Proteins are digested in the stomach and most digestion and absorption occur in the small intestine.
concepts.rule: In the stomach the walls contract and relax to churn the food, which mixes with a secretion of digestive juice, acid and mucus. The digestive juice breaks down proteins; the acid helps this and kills many harmful bacteria; mucus protects the stomach lining. Food becomes a semi-liquid mass. The small intestine, about 6 metres long, is the longest part of the alimentary canal. It receives digestive secretions from its own lining, the liver and the pancreas. The liver secretes bile, mildly basic, which neutralises acids and breaks fats into tiny droplets. The pancreas secretes pancreatic juice, also basic, which breaks down carbohydrates, proteins and fats. The intestinal wall's juice further breaks down fats, proteins and partially digested carbohydrates. Digested nutrients pass into the blood in the walls of the small intestine, called absorption; thousands of finger-like projections increase the surface area for absorption. In 1822 Dr William Beaumont observed digestion in Alexis St. Martin's stomach through a permanent wound.
concepts.example: Celiac disease damages the small intestine lining and millets are gluten-free alternatives.

concepts.name: Large intestine, egestion and healthy digestion
concepts.description: Water absorption, stool, rectum, egestion, fibre, fermented foods and healthy eating habits.
concepts.idea: The large intestine absorbs water and salts, and undigested waste leaves the body by egestion.
concepts.rule: Undigested food moves into the large intestine, about 1.5 metres long, shorter than the small intestine but wider, hence called large. It absorbs water and some salts from the undigested food, making the waste semi-solid, called stool. The stool is stored in the rectum, the lower part of the large intestine, and expelled through the anus in a process called egestion. Fibre-rich foods like fruits, vegetables and whole grains help the large intestine function and make the stool easier to pass. The large intestine has bacteria that help digestion by breaking down undigested food, especially fibre, and making some nutrients; fermented foods such as curd, buttermilk, kanji, gundruk and poita bhat are good for the digestive system. The Charaka Samhita highlights easily digestible foods and spices like ginger, black pepper and cumin. Good habits: eat at proper times, eat mindfully and avoid overeating.
concepts.example: Curd and buttermilk are fermented foods that support digestion.

concepts.name: Digestion in ruminants and birds
concepts.description: Rumination in cows and buffaloes, and the gizzard in birds.
concepts.idea: Animals show variations in the alimentary canal to digest different kinds of food.
concepts.rule: Grass-eating animals such as cows and buffaloes partly chew the grass and swallow it into the stomach, where partial digestion takes place. The partially digested food is brought back to the mouth for gradual chewing. This is rumination, and such animals are called ruminants. A cow spends about 8 hours a day chewing its food, which then passes down the alimentary canal for further digestion. Birds have no teeth but have a chamber called the gizzard where the food is broken down by contraction and relaxation of its walls, often with the help of grit (small stones) they swallow. Thus animals differ in the structure and function of the alimentary canal to suit different ways of digesting different foods.
concepts.example: A cow chews even when not grazing because it is ruminating.

concepts.name: Breathing and the human respiratory system
concepts.description: The pathway of air, alveoli, mechanism of inhalation and exhalation, the model and exhaled air.
concepts.idea: Breathing moves air into and out of the lungs through the respiratory system.
concepts.rule: Breathing is inhaling and exhaling air. Without breathing we usually cannot survive more than a few minutes. The respiratory system begins with the nostrils, then the nasal passages, where hair and mucus trap dust and dirt, so we should breathe through the nose. Air reaches the lungs through the windpipe, which branches into two, one to each lung, ending in small balloon-like sacs called alveoli. The rib cage protects the lungs. On inhalation the ribs move up and outwards and the diaphragm, a dome-shaped muscle below the lungs, moves down, increasing space in the chest so air enters. On exhalation the ribs move down and inwards and the diaphragm moves up, pushing air out. In the model (Activity 9.2) the balloons represent the lungs and the rubber sheet the diaphragm. In Activity 9.3 exhaled air turns lime water milky, showing it contains more carbon dioxide than inhaled air. Smoking damages lungs, and passive smoking harms others.
concepts.example: Pranayama and deep breathing improve lung health and relaxation.

concepts.name: Respiration, gas exchange and the circulatory system
concepts.description: Respiration as breakdown of glucose with oxygen, the word equation, breathing versus respiration, alveoli exchange and circulation.
concepts.idea: Respiration releases energy from glucose using oxygen; breathing is a physical process and respiration a chemical one.
concepts.rule: Food is broken down to simple substances such as glucose, and oxygen helps break down glucose to release energy. This is respiration: Glucose + Oxygen gives Carbon dioxide + Water + Energy. Inhaled air has nearly 21% oxygen and 0.04% carbon dioxide, and exhaled air has nearly 16-17% oxygen and 4-5% carbon dioxide, so not all oxygen is used. In the alveoli, whose thin walls are surrounded by fine blood tubes, oxygen passes into the blood and carbon dioxide from the blood passes into the alveoli to be exhaled. Breathing brings in oxygen and removes carbon dioxide and is a physical process; respiration uses oxygen to release energy in the cells and is a chemical process. The circulatory system, which includes the heart, blood and blood vessels, carries nutrients, oxygen and other substances to all parts and carries wastes away. The energy lets us walk, run, play and think.
concepts.example: After running, breathing becomes faster because the body needs more energy.

concepts.name: Breathing in different animals
concepts.description: Lungs, gills, skin and adaptations to habitat in birds, fish, amphibians and earthworms.
concepts.idea: Different animals have different breathing organs that suit their habitats.
concepts.rule: Birds, elephants, lions, cows, goats, lizards and snakes breathe with lungs, though the structure of their lungs differs. Most aquatic animals such as fish have gills, structures richly supplied with blood vessels, where oxygen and carbon dioxide are exchanged between the blood and the gases dissolved in water. Amphibians like frogs use different parts at different stages: tadpoles breathe through gills, and adult frogs use lungs on land and skin for gas exchange when in water. Earthworms use their moist skin for the exchange of oxygen and carbon dioxide. Thus different animals have different breathing mechanisms to suit their habitats. The digestive, respiratory and circulatory systems work in coordination with others to sustain life.
concepts.example: Birds fly at high altitudes where oxygen is low.
